subject: Throughput anchoring and token-velocity calibration — follow-up & action items
messages:
From: Diego Fernandez <diego_fernandez@redwood.com>
To: Alex Chen <alex@shipwell.com>, Courtney Li <courtney@shipwell.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-22T17:12:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call: throughput anchoring & token-velocity calibration (recap)

Hi Alex / Courtney —

Thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and the asks we agreed on so we can size proposal work: 

Summary of what we heard
- App pattern: mix of short generation calls (single-response text generation) plus streaming sessions for multi-step workflows.
- Steady-state expectation: moderate QPS during business hours.
- Burst behavior: occasional short lived spikes (1–3 minutes) tied to batch imports and marketing events.
- Latency expectation: interactive feel for streaming first-token latency; control-plane SLOs for straightforward generations.

Action items for Shipwell (what we'd like from you)
1) Provide a 48–72 hour sample of production traffic (timestamped request log) or a synthesized traffic_profile.csv with per-request tokens_in, tokens_out, streaming_flag, and duration.
2) Confirm steady-state QPS and top-10 peak windows (start/end timestamps + observed QPS) if available.
3) Percent of requests that use streaming vs single-response (approx %).

Quick questions to clarify sizing
- For streaming sessions, what is the average sustained tokens/sec after the first token?
- For generation-only calls, do you have an average prompt + expected completion token count?

We'll take your sample and run a token-velocity model to estimate: steady capacity (QPS), recommended burst headroom, and a mapping to latency SLOs (p50/p95 first token and total completion).

Attachments: I attached a small example JSON schema (shipwell_peak_sample.json) and a CSV template (traffic_profile.csv) to make the sample easier to provide.

Proposed next step
- If you can share the sample by EOD Friday (2028-07-26), we can return a preliminary sizing and recommended config by Tuesday 2028-07-30.

Thanks — happy to jump on a short follow-up if helpful.

Diego Fernandez
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
N: +1 415-555-0199
Redwood Inference

Attachments: shipwell_peak_sample.json (application/json stub), traffic_profile.csv (text/csv stub)

From: Alex Chen <alex@shipwell.com>

Date: 2028-07-24T09:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: throughput anchoring & token-velocity calibration (recap)

Diego — thanks for the recap and the templates. Quick answers below (see inline).

On Jul 22, 2028, at 5:12 PM, Diego Fernandez wrote:
> We'll take your sample and run a token-velocity model to estimate...

Steady-state / peaks
- Typical steady-state QPS: ~12 QPS during peak business hours (US PST).
- Average tokens per request (prompt + completion): ~320 tokens.
- Peak windows: we observe short spikes up to ~420 QPS lasting ~90–180s during nightly batch loads and some customer sync events. Those are rare (maybe 6–8 times per month).

Streaming
- ~18% of user sessions use streaming. Of those, ~60% are long-lived (>=45s), average sustained tokens/sec during streaming ~6 t/s after initial ramp.

Latency SLOs
- Internal target for interactive sessions: first-token <= 250ms (p50) and p95 <= 700ms.
- For non-interactive batch generations we can accept higher tail latency (p95 <= 3s).

Privacy/Logs
- We can share an anonymized 72-hour request sample — removing user IDs and payloads, keeping token counts and timestamps. Attaching a small extract now (see shipwell_peak_sample.json) and will produce the CSV by Thursday.

Let me know if you need different fields in the CSV template.

—Alex
Alex Chen
Platform Engineering, Shipwell
alex@shipwell.com

Attachments included: shipwell_peak_sample.json (redacted extract)

From: Diego Fernandez <diego_fernandez@redwood.com>
To: Alex Chen <alex@shipwell.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-26T15:28:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: throughput anchoring & token-velocity calibration (recap)

Alex — great, the extract is perfect and matches what we need. A couple follow-ups as we start modeling: 

1) Burst sizing assumption: given rare short spikes to ~420 QPS for ~2 minutes, do you have an SLA requirement for availability/latency during those spikes or is graceful degradation acceptable (e.g., higher tail latencies for <5% of traffic)?

2) Percent streaming long sessions: when you say ~60% of streaming sessions are >=45s, can you estimate average total tokens per long-session (including initial prompts)? That drives KV cache lifetimes and memory sizing.

Preliminary estimate (very rough) based on the extract and your numbers:
- Steady baseline: 12 QPS * 320 tokens/request -> ~3840 tokens/sec
- Peak short bursts: 420 QPS * 320 tokens/request -> ~134400 tokens/sec (for the burst window)
- Streaming sustained: 18% of sessions with avg sustained 6 t/s across 60% long sessions -> additional concurrent token throughput to account for in capacity model

Suggested short-term approach
- For a pilot: target capacity to handle steady-state with a 2.5x buffer (handles moderate day-to-day variance) and define an explicit fallback policy for ultra-short spikes (offload to queued processing or increased timeout windows).
- For production: plan a burst headroom policy (automated scale to cover up to 420 QPS for 180s) if you need strict latency SLOs during spikes.

Next actions we will take
- Marissa will run the token-velocity model against your CSV and return a resource estimate (GPU counts, suggested batch sizes, and recommended quantization/profile) by Monday 2028-07-29.
- I'll prepare an A/B rollback plan and an initial mutual action plan (MAP) draft for dedicated/reserved capacity options.

Can you confirm the SLA tolerance for the short bursts and provide the average tokens per long streaming session by EOD 2028-07-27?

Thanks — Diego

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Date: 2028-07-28T10:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: throughput anchoring & token-velocity calibration (recap)

Alex / Diego — quick update from the Redwood side after a first pass on the extract Alex sent: 

What we ran
- Token-velocity model over the 72hr extract to compute steady vs. burst token/sec distributions and concurrency windows.

Preliminary findings (summary)
- Baseline tokens/sec (median): ~3.9k t/s, matches Diego's back-of-envelope.
- Short burst toes (99th percentile windows): equivalent to ~110–130k t/s depending on clustering of peaks — which aligns with the 420 QPS * approx token estimate but reduced slightly due to partial short-request mix.
- Streaming long sessions materially increase memory (KV) requirements; each long-session at 6 t/s with average 60s duration implies ~360 tokens/session in-flight on average.

Redwood action items (we own these)
1) Produce a recommendation: pilot capacity (GPU types + count), expected steady vs. burst costs, and recommended runtime config (batch sizes, kv cache TTLs) — delivery Monday 2028-07-29.
2) Prepare a short MAP that includes: pilot scope, success metrics (latency p50/p95 targets), burst tolerance thresholds, and rollback triggers.
3) Offer a short follow-up call on Tuesday 2028-07-30 to walk the sizing and MAP.

Questions for Shipwell
- Confirm whether strict first-token p95 during bursts is a hard requirement. If yes, we will size for active scaling to cover 420 QPS bursts rather than fallback.

Thanks — will have a more detailed packet Monday.

Marissa Cole
Performance & SRE Lead, Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com
Redwood Inference
